parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem: Fluorine-18 ($^{18}_{9}\text{F}$) is an isotope that decays to an isotope of oxygen (O) by the emission of a $\beta^{+}$ particle.
parts.text:
Complete the nuclear equation for the decay, including all the particles involved.
$$^{18}_{9}\text{F} \rightarrow$$
hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens inside the nucleus in beta-plus decay - a proton turns into a neutron, so how do the total nucleon number $A$ and the proton number $Z$ change?
Hint 2: Balance the charge on both sides. The oxygen nucleus has one fewer proton than fluorine, so the emitted beta particle must carry away that positive charge - recall its $A$ and $Z$ numbers.
Hint 3: Remember lepton number must also balance. A positron alone is not enough, so a second very light neutral lepton is also emitted alongside it.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Keep track of nucleons**
In any beta decay the total number of nucleons stays the same because a proton simply changes into a neutron inside the nucleus. So $A$ stays at 18. The daughter is an isotope of oxygen, which always has $Z = 8$. That gives $^{18}_{8}\text{O}$ on the right.

Step 2: **Add the positron to balance charge**
Fluorine has $Z = 9$ and oxygen has $Z = 8$. The lost positive charge is carried by the $\beta^{+}$ particle, the positron: $$^{0}_{+1}\beta$$ It has nucleon number 0 and charge +1, so proton number balances as $9 = 8 + 1$.

Step 3: **Add the neutrino to complete the decay**
Beta-plus decay always emits an electron neutrino $^{0}_{0}\nu_{e}$ as well to conserve energy, momentum and lepton number. The full balanced equation is: $$^{18}_{9}\text{F} \rightarrow ^{18}_{8}\text{O} + ^{0}_{+1}\beta + ^{0}_{0}\nu_{e}$$

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: A quark in the fluorine-18 nucleus changes flavour during the decay. State this change of flavour.
hints: Hint 1: Picture a proton as $uud$ and a neutron as $udd$. In this decay a proton becomes a neutron, so which quark flavour must have changed?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Look inside the proton**
A proton is $uud$ and a neutron is $udd$. Beta-plus decay turns a proton into a neutron, so one of the $u$ quarks with charge $+2/3e$ must turn into a $d$ quark with charge $-1/3e$. That is an up quark to a down quark change.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: A hadron has a charge of $-2e$, where $e$ is the elementary charge.
parts.text: State and explain whether the hadron is a meson or a baryon.

markscheme_points.text: must be three (anti)quarks as largest (negative) quark charge;
or mesons can only have a charge of 0 or $\pm 1(e)$; (so hadron is) a baryon

hints: Hint 1: Recall the make-up: a meson is one quark plus one antiquark, while a baryon is three quarks (or three antiquarks). Think about the largest charge magnitude you can build from just two quarks.
Hint 2: Check the quark charges: $+2/3e$, $-1/3e$ and the opposite for antiquarks. Can any quark-antiquark pair add to $-2e$? What does that tell you about the hadron type?
parts.proper_answer: Baryon, as a meson (quark-antiquark pair) can only have charge 0 or $\pm 1e$, so charge $-2e$ requires three (anti)quarks.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Compare possible meson charges**
A meson is made of a quark and an antiquark. With charges of $\pm 2/3e$ and $\pm 1/3e$, the most negative combination you can make is e.g. $d + \bar{u} = -1/3e -2/3e = -1e$. So a meson can only have charge $0$ or $\pm 1e$.

Step 2: **Identify the hadron**
A charge of $-2e$ is impossible for a meson. It must be made of three (anti)quarks, which means it is a baryon (in this case made of three antiquarks).

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: State a possible quark composition for the hadron.

markscheme_points.text: any combination of three from: antiup (quark) / up antiquark and/or anticharm (quark) / charm antiquark and/or antitop (quark) / top antiquark

hints: Hint 1: You need three antiquarks that each contribute negative charge to total $-2e$. Which antiquarks carry $-2/3e$?
parts.proper_answer: Any three of anti-up / anti-charm / anti-top, e.g. $\bar{u}\bar{u}\bar{u}$ giving $3 \times (-2/3e) = -2e$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Pick three $-2/3e$ antiquarks**
To get $-2e$ you need three antiquarks each of charge $-2/3e$. The $u$, $c$ and $t$ quarks have $+2/3e$, so their antiquarks $\bar{u}$, $\bar{c}$, $\bar{t}$ have $-2/3e$. Any combination of three works, for example: $$\bar{u} + \bar{u} + \bar{u} = -2/3e -2/3e -2/3e = -2e$$
